h1: Hiring a brewpub chef who understands beer
title: Hiring a Brewpub Chef Who Gets Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: What beer knowledge to look for in a brewpub chef, how to test it at interview and how to get kitchen and brewhouse working as one team.
teaser: Good cooking is easy to find. A chef who writes a menu around your taps is not.
standfirst: In a brewpub the kitchen decides how long a table stays and what it drinks. Here is what beer understanding looks like in a chef, how to test for it and how to keep the chef and the brewer pulling the same way.
sections: In a brewpub the kitchen sells the beer

Most tables in an Indian brewpub order food with their beer. The kitchen decides how long those tables stay. A chef who treats beer as just another bar item writes a menu that fights the taps. Delicate fish sits next to a 60 IBU IPA. Sweet desserts arrive with nothing on the list to match them.

What you want is a cook who thinks about the glass on the table while writing the plate. That is rarer than good cooking. Most chefs in India train in hotels and restaurants where wine and cocktails get the pairing attention. Beer is the lager in the fridge. You are hiring for a skill most candidates have never been asked to show.
What beer understanding looks like in a chef

You are not looking for a brewer. You are looking for someone who knows how beer behaves next to food:

  • Bitterness and alcohol amplify chilli heat. A hoppy pale ale with a fiery vindaloo can be punishing, while a softer wheat beer calms it.
  • Carbonation and bitterness cut fat, which is why a crisp lager works with pakoras and fried chicken.
  • Malt sweetness meets caramelised and roasted flavours: tandoori meats, grilled paneer, a brown ale with a mutton sukka.
  • Roast in a stout sits well with chocolate and coffee desserts.
  • Acidity in a sour beer works like a squeeze of lime on chaat.

A chef who cooks with beer should also know that bitterness concentrates as liquid reduces. Reduce a 60 IBU IPA by half for a sauce and it turns harsh. Malty, low bitterness beers suit batters, braises and glazes. Our guide to brewpub food menus and margins covers the menu side.
Test the palate in the interview, not the CV

A CV tells you where someone cooked. It does not tell you whether they can taste. Run a short trial instead.

Pour three of your house beers in small measures, for example a wheat beer around 5% ABV, your IPA and a stout. Ask the candidate to describe each in their own words and propose a dish for each one. Then give them one beer from your list, a budget and your kitchen for an hour and ask for a single plate built around it. Watch the station as closely as the plate: hygiene, organisation and pace during service matter more than one clever dish.

Some excellent chefs do not drink. Tasting a few sips and spitting is enough for pairing work, so ask how a candidate would approach it rather than ruling anyone out.
Costing matters as much as flavour

A beer-literate chef who cannot cost a dish will sink your margins. Many brewpub kitchens aim for a food cost somewhere around 28 to 35% of menu price. Ask candidates to cost one of their own dishes in the interview. A plate that sells at ₹450 with ₹140 of ingredients runs at about 31%. Someone who can do that sum without a calculator, then tell you how they would bring it down, has run a real kitchen.

Ask about wastage too. A chef who plans prep to the weekly covers forecast and reuses trim sensibly saves more money than one who cooks beautifully and orders by feel.
Make the chef and the brewer work as one team

The pairing only works if the kitchen knows what is coming out of the tanks. Have the brewer share the tank plan three to four weeks ahead. An ale is usually ready in two to three weeks and a lager takes longer, so the specials board can follow the brew schedule rather than chase it. Taste every new beer together the day it goes on tap.

Spent grain is the shared ingredient most brewpubs waste. Fresh from the mash tun it is roughly 75 to 80% water and in Indian heat it sours within a day or two. A chef who has a plan for it, in breads, crackers or a dog biscuit for regulars, must collect it on brew day and dry or use it fast.
The terms and the first 90 days

Agree the scope in writing: head chef or senior cook, who orders, who signs off menu changes and who owns food cost. A probation period, often three to six months, gives both sides a way out. Check food safety training as well. FSSAI expects licensed food businesses to have a trained food safety supervisor. A chef who already holds that training saves you a step.

Hiring is half the problem. Writing a role that ties kitchen numbers to the whole brewpub's numbers is the other half. Founders usually learn that part by losing money. Your first step: write a one page brief listing your core beers with their ABV and IBU, plus the two dishes you most want each beer to sell. Use it as the tasting sheet for every interview.
faqs: Does a brewpub chef need to know how beer is brewed?
No. They need to know how beer behaves with food: bitterness, carbonation, malt sweetness, roast and acidity. Brewing knowledge is a bonus.
How do I test a chef's beer palate?
Pour three house beers in small measures, ask the candidate to describe each and suggest a dish. Then have them cook one plate for one of your beers in your kitchen.
What food cost should a brewpub kitchen aim for?
Many brewpub kitchens aim for roughly 28 to 35% of menu price. Your own target depends on rent, menu style and how much the bar contributes.
